item.title: [1.8] Transcriptional upregulation of NDUFA10 by ATF3 sustains mitochondrial bioenergetics and malignant phenotypes in NSCLC
item.description:
Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a leading cause of global cancer mortality, necessitating the identification of novel therapeutic vulnerabilities. This study identifies NDUFA10, a key mitochondrial Complex I subunit, as a critical driver of NSCLC pathogenesis. Multi-cohort analysis of TCGA and clinical datasets revealed significant NDUFA10 upregulation in neoplastic tissues, which correlated with advanced pathological stage, metastasis, smoking history, and poor overall survival. Single-cell RNA sequencing further localized NDUFA10 enrichment to proliferating malignant epithelial subpopulations, where its expression positively associated with oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and ATP synthesis across primary and metastatic sites. Functionally, NDUFA10 ablation (shRNA or CRISPR/Cas9) in primary NSCLC and A549 cells disrupted mitochondrial homeostasis—evidenced by impaired respiration, attenuated Complex I activity, and augmented ROS production—while inhibiting cell viability, migration, and invasion. Mechanistically, NDUFA10 modulates the Akt-mTOR signaling axis; constitutively active Akt1 partially rescued the proliferative and survival deficits induced by NDUFA10 silencing. Furthermore, intersectional bioinformatics and ChIP-qPCR identified ATF3 as the direct transcriptional activator driving NDUFA10 overexpression. In vivo, NDUFA10-silenced xenografts exhibited significantly attenuated growth, characterized by compromised mitochondrial function and inhibited Akt-mTOR activation. In summary, our findings characterize NDUFA10 as a critical metabolic checkpoint in NSCLC, where its ATF3-driven its overexpression coordinates mitochondrial bioenergetics and Akt-mTOR signaling to sustain malignant progression.

item.title: [1.7] HSPB8 regulates CTP synthase filaments to couple nucleotide metabolism and autophagy in tumors
item.description:
Metabolic adaptation and proteostasis are essential for tumor survival under nutrient stress, yet how these processes are mechanistically integrated remains unclear. Here, we identify CTP synthase (CTPS) filament dynamics as a regulatory nexus linking nucleotide metabolism to autophagic flux. Under glutamine deprivation—a hallmark of poorly vascularized solid tumors—CTPS undergoes polymerization into filamentous assemblies that exhibit reduced enzymatic activity. We demonstrate that filament formation is driven by intracellular asparagine availability and regulated by the accumulation of misfolded proteins. Using APEX2-based proximity labeling and proteomics, we identify the small heat shock protein HSPB8 as a filament-associated regulator. HSPB8, acting within the chaperone-assisted selective autophagy (CASA) pathway, antagonizes CTPS polymerization by promoting clearance of misfolded proteins, thereby restoring soluble, catalytically active CTPS. Filament disassembly increases CTP production and enhances synthesis of autophagy-related phospholipids, including phosphatidylinositol and phosphatidylethanolamine, resulting in accelerated autophagic flux. Cells expressing filament-deficient CTPS mutants display elevated autophagosome formation and increased LC3-II accumulation upon lysosomal blockade, confirming enhanced flux. In vivo, disruption of CTPS filament assembly impairs xenograft tumor growth and is associated with excessive autophagy. Analysis of TCGA datasets further reveals that high CTPS and low HSPB8 expression correlate with poor patient survival across multiple cancers. Collectively, our findings establish CTPS filament dynamics as a proteostasis-sensitive metabolic switch that coordinates nucleotide biosynthesis with autophagy, revealing a previously unrecognized vulnerability in tumors adapting to nutrient limitation.

item.title: [1.7] Normalized membrane ratio of TROP2 as a predictor of clinical outcomes with datopotamab deruxtecan in non-small-cell lung cancer
item.description:
Datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd)—a trophoblast cell surface antigen 2 (TROP2)-directed antibody–drug conjugate—has demonstrated efficacy in patients with advanced nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) ± actionable genomic alterations. However, TROP2 expression by pathologist assessment using conventional immunohistochemistry with visual scoring does not predict response to TROP2-directed antibody–drug conjugates in NSCLC. We developed TROP2 quantitative continuous scoring (QCS)—a fully supervised computational pathology approach that quantifies TROP2 expression in individual NSCLC cells and subcellular components from immunohistochemistry-stained slides. Using QCS to determine TROP2 expression at the tumor cell membrane and cytoplasm, normalized membrane ratio (NMR) was developed (ratio of membrane relative to membrane + cytoplasmic TROP2) in the biomarker-evaluable population of patients with advanced NSCLC in the TROPION-PanTumor01 study (n = 115). The TROP2 NMR cut-point was optimized and validated in patients with nonsquamous NSCLC without actionable genomic alterations (primary intended-use population, n = 221) in the biomarker-evaluable population (n = 352) of the TROPION-Lung01 trial. Association with clinical outcomes was assessed. Progression-free survival was longer in Dato-DXd-treated (median 7.2 versus 4.0 months; hazard ratio 0.40, 95% confidence interval 0.25–0.64) but not docetaxel-treated (median 4.1 versus 4.4 months; hazard ratio 0.94, 95% confidence interval 0.59–1.49) patients with TROP2 NMR-positive versus TROP2 NMR-negative samples (treatment by biomarker status interaction P = 0.0098), indicating that TROP2 NMR may be a predictive biomarker for Dato-DXd. This work developed and validated a computational pathology biomarker—the TROP2 normalized membrane ratio—that quantifies subcellular TROP2 localization and predicts improved progression-free and overall survival with datopotamab deruxtecan in patients with nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer lacking actionable genomic alterations.

item.title: [2.0] Lysine 69 deacetylation of NFIC drives autophagy-induced epithelial–mesenchymal transition and chemoresistance in glioblastoma
item.description:
Acquired temozolomide (TMZ) resistance is a major obstacle in improving glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) treatment. Accumulating evidence has indicated that autophagy has dual effects on the regulation of chemoresistance. In our previous study, we reported that autophagic inducers can upregulate the E3 ligase HERC3 and then mediate TMZ resistance by activating the HERC3/SMAD7/TGF-β pathway. However, the underlying mechanism within the increasing expression of HERC3 induced by autophagy is still unknown. Herein, we show that autophagy promotes the deacetylation of nuclear factor I C (NFIC) at lysine 69, which induces the transcriptional activation of forkhead box protein K1 (FOXK1) and thus promotes HERC3 dependent epithelial‒mesenchymal transition (EMT). The dynamic equilibrium of NFIC K69Ac is controlled by the acetyltransferase P300 and the deacetylase HDAC6. Pe-k69, a cell-penetrating peptide, can specifically block NFIC K69 deacetylation and sensitise GBM cells to TMZ. Our study reveals an acetylation-dependent regulatory mechanism, which may provide mechanistic clues for targeting NFIC to overcome GBM chemoresistance. Autophagy-induced the deacetylation of NFIC at Lysine 69 site accelerates tumorigenesis by activating FOXK1/HERC3 axis, revealing an acetylation-dependent mechanism that can be targeted by peptide Pe-k69 to overcome TMZ resistance in glioblastoma.

item.title: [2.0] Synergistic effect of XYL-1 and Olaparib in BRCA-proficient TNBC cells is associated with RAD51 and BRCA1 downregulation
item.description:
Poly-ADP-ribose polymerase1/2 (PARP1/2) inhibitors are approved for HER2-negative breast cancer harboring germline BRCA1/2 mutations, including TNBC. However, the majority of patients with BRCA-proficient derive limited benefit from these agents. In this study, we demonstrate that the efficacy of the PARP1/2 inhibitor Olaparib in BRCA-proficient TNBC cell lines can be markedly enhanced by co-treatment with the PARP7 inhibitor XYL-1. Our results demonstrated that the combination of Olaparib and XYL-1 significantly inhibited the proliferation of BRCA-proficient MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells compared with either monotherapy, with the strongest synergistic effect observed at a 1:1 molar ratio in MDA-MB-231 cells. Furthermore, the combination of Olaparib and XYL-1 significantly increased cellular ROS levels, induced DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), and ultimately promoted apoptosis. In vivo, the combined treatment significantly suppressed MDA-MB-231 tumor growth compared with either monotherapy, while exhibiting a favorable safety profile. Mechanistically, co-treatment with XYL-1 and Olaparib significantly downregulated RAD51 and BRCA1 expression, which may be associated with impaired homologous recombination (HR)-mediated DNA repair. Collectively, these findings suggest that dual targeting of PARP7 and PARP1/2 represents a promising combination strategy for the treatment of BRCA-proficient TNBC.

item.title: [1.6] Mitochondrial protein import defects enhance tumour immunogenicity
item.description:
Tumour cells evade detection and elimination by the immune system through a suite of adaptations1, including the repression of antigen presentation, which is required for the recognition of tumour cells by CD8+ T cells. Mitochondria have emerged as targets for enhancing antitumour immunity; however, the extensive mitochondrial proteome has remained largely unstudied for its ability to modulate immune responses. Here we show that defects in the mitochondrial protein import machinery promote tumour immunogenicity and synergize with immune checkpoint blockade treatment in melanoma models. Mitochondrial protein import perturbation, specifically through depletion of the TIM23 import complex subunit TIMM50, enhances tumour immunogenicity through a pathway involving mitochondrial DNA escape, cGAS–STING pathway activation and interferon-β (IFNβ) secretion. Secreted IFNβ signals through the type I IFN receptor to activate the JAK–STAT pathway, resulting in increased antigen presentation on MHC class I complexes. Mitochondrial DNA escape in Timm50-depleted cells is linked to the formation of mitochondrial-derived vesicles. Depletion of SNX9 and RAB9, involved in mitochondrial-derived vesicle formation2, suppresses mitochondrial DNA-dependent type I IFN production and signalling. By disrupting mitochondrial proteostasis and membrane architecture, defective protein import in Timm50-depleted cells drives the immune phenotype. This study shows that mitochondrial protein import inhibition causes tumour immunogenicity, including sensitization to immune checkpoint blockade, by promoting mitochondrial DNA escape and IFNβ-driven MHC class I antigen presentation. Inhibition of mitochondrial protein import can enhance tumour immunogenicity by promoting mitochondrial DNA release.

item.title: [1.6] Serum extracellular vesicle proteomics reveals treatment-associated biomarkers in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
item.description:
Background Longitudinal biomarkers of treatment response in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) are needed. Extracellular vesicle (EV)-enriched serum proteomics may provide a minimally invasive approach for monitoring systemic and tumor-associated responses to therapy. Methods Paired pre-treatment and post-treatment serum samples were analyzed from 51 patients with pancreatic cancer, including 25 treated with FOLFIRINOX and 20 treated with gemcitabine-based therapy. EVs were enriched using the Mag-Net method and profiled by data independent acquisition mass spectrometry. After batch correction and filtering, 941 proteins were retained for differential and pathway analyses. Paired linear models and gene set enrichment analyses were used to assess treatment-associated changes. Baseline protein abundance and longitudinal changes were evaluated in relation to overall survival (OS) using Cox models. Results A total of 2,089 EV-associated proteins were identified, with an average of 1,186 proteins quantified per sample. Across the cohort, 26 proteins differed between post- and pretreatment samples. Proteins that increased after treatment were primarily related to extracellular matrix organization and cell adhesion, whereas proteins that decreased after treatment were associated with actin cytoskeletal organization, coagulation, and hemostasis. Treatment-associated changes were more pronounced in the FOLFIRINOX group, in which 32 proteins were differentially expressed. FOLFIRINOX was characterized by coordinated reductions in platelet- and coagulation-associated proteins, including PF4, PF4V1, PPBP, GP5, ITGA2B, and ITGB3, accompanied by enrichment of platelet activation, coagulation, and hemostasis pathways among down-regulated processes. No individual proteins met the same significance threshold in the gemcitabine group. A composite seven-protein platelet score decreased significantly after FOLFIRINOX but not for gemcitabine, and the between-regimen difference in score change was significant. Higher pretreatment ITGB1 abundance was associated with longer OS after multiple-testing correction (HR, 0.112; BH-FDR = 0.0063). In multivariable analysis, greater treatment-associated platelet-score depletion was independently associated with shorter OS (HR per unit increase in {Delta}score, 0.56; P = 0.030). Conclusions Longitudinal serum EV-enriched proteomics identified treatment-associated biological changes in PDAC, including a coordinated platelet-related response predominantly observed after FOLFIRINOX. Baseline ITGB1 abundance and longitudinal platelet-score changes represent potentially complementary prognostic and pharmacodynamic markers. These findings are exploratory and require validation in larger, independent cohorts incorporating platelet counts, coagulation measurements, and targeted proteomic assays.

item.title: [1.6] Genotype-Informed Drosophila Kinome Screening Prioritizes PRKX as a Candidate Vulnerability in Bladder Cancer
item.description:
Muscle-invasive bladder cancer is molecularly heterogeneous, and the basal/squamous subtype frequently exhibits elevated EGFR expression and TP53 and RB1 alterations. Functional vulnerabilities associated with these alterations remain incompletely defined, while large-scale in vivo screening in mammalian models is experimentally demanding. Therefore, we developed a genotype-defined Drosophila melanogaster model combining Egfr overexpression, mutant p53, and Rbf suppression in Malpighian tubules. The resulting 3-hit model showed increased Malpighian tubule volume and reduced adult eclosion rate. A dominant modifier screen targeting 216 kinase genes identified 72 genes whose perturbation significantly increased the eclosion rate, and a complementary RNA interference screen identified eight kinases whose knockdown increased the eclosion rate. Among these hits, Pka-C3, which is a Drosophila ortholog of human PRKX, emerged as one of the strongest suppressors of the 3-hit phenotype. PRKX was prioritized for further study because public transcriptomic datasets showed higher PRKX expression in bladder tumors than in normal bladder tissue. PRKX knockdown reduced spheroid volume in four human bladder cancer cell lines with distinct EGFR, TP53, and RB1 profiles. Both small interfering RNAs produced significant reductions in two cell lines, whereas only one siRNA reached significance in the other two. These findings nominate PRKX as a candidate vulnerability in bladder cancer and highlight a cross-species approach that combines genotype-informed Drosophila screening with functional testing in human cancer cells to prioritize targets for further investigation.

item.title: [1.8] The Phospholipase A2 Activity of Peroxiredoxin 6 Protects Hepatocarcinoma Cells Against Ferroptosis and Mitophagy Impairment
item.description:
Peroxiredoxin 6 (PRDX6) is a moonlighting protein that plays a key role in regulating redox homeostasis and lipid metabolism through its unique dual peroxidase and calcium-independent phospholipase A2 (iPLA2) activities. Here, we generated a stable HepG2 cell line harboring a D140A mutation to selectively ablate iPLA2 activity, and we compared its phenotype with that of wild-type (WT) and PRDX6-knockout (KO) cells. D140A exhibited low ROS leves, similar to WT cells, confirming that oxidative stress is due to peroxidase deficiency. In contrast, D140A cells displayed higher lipid peroxidation than WT cells, though significantly lower than that of KO cells. Furthermore, the D140A mutant mirrored the KO phenotype regarding intracellular ferrous iron accumulation, impaired lipid droplet biogenesis, and the downregulation of the key ferroptosis regulator GPX4. Mechanistically, integrated proteomic, lipidomic, and enzymatic analyses revealed that a deficiency in iPLA2 activity of PRDX6 disrupted the release of key lipid species necessary for cell structure and signaling. Consequently, organelles involved in lipid synthesis and trafficking, such as peroxisomes, endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria and lipid droplet, were affected. Specifically, we found that mitochondria exhibited a reduction in cristae and a diminished capacity for mitophagy and autophagy, which ultimately makes cells much more susceptible to erastin-induced ferroptotic cell death. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that PRDX6 iPLA2 activity uniquely coordinates organelle lipid homeostasis and mitophagy to protect cancer cells from ferroptotic cell death. Consequently, the use of iPLA2 inhibitors such as MJ33, which decreased PRDX6 iPLA2 activity to a level comparable to the mutant D140A, could represent a promising therapeutic strategy for inducing ferroptotic cell death in hepatocellular carcinoma.

item.title: [1.8] Cancer drug resistance as a temporal process: cell plasticity, adaptive buffering, signaling pathways and therapeutic interception
item.description:
Cancer drug resistance remains a principal barrier to durable cancer control, yet it is still often interpreted through endpoint-centred models that emphasise pre-existing resistant clones, incomplete drug exposure or late-acquired mechanisms. These explanations are essential but incomplete. The question is not only why resistant cells exist, but also how residual cells remain alive long enough to become resistant. Across tumour types and therapeutic modalities, treatment reshapes residual populations while it is acting, driving transitions through non-genetic heterogeneity, stochastic cell-fate variability, reversible tolerance, stress adaptation, microenvironmental support and eventually stable resistance. This Review develops a temporal framework in which resistance is resolved into a phase-structured trajectory organised around two mechanistic transitions: entry into adaptive buffering and later stabilisation into resistance hardening. Adaptive buffering is defined operationally as a transient, support-dependent survival state in which residual tumour cells preserve viability by recruiting physiological support systems while molecular and phenotypic reorganisation proceeds. It is not a single pathway or a synonym for drug tolerance, but a functional demand-capacity state whose dependencies change over time. We distinguish adaptive buffering from drug tolerance, persister states, dormancy, minimal residual disease and established resistance and discuss how buffering can be evaluated experimentally using perturbational, single-cell, spatial, computational and functional readouts. The framework suggests that informative biomarkers should assign residual populations to adaptive phases, so that therapy can intercept transient dependencies before adaptive states become hardened and clinically entrenched.

item.title: [1.6] Microbiota-based modulation of intratumoral cholesterol metabolism for colorectal cancer treatment
item.description:
Excess cholesterol accumulates in colorectal cancer (CRC) and promotes its progression, yet systemic cholesterol-lowering has limited benefits and safety concerns. Here we show that redirecting intestinal cholesterol metabolism through the gut microbiota generates a metabolite, 4-cholesten-3-one (4-C-3), which suppresses CRC growth. A screen of microbial cholesterol metabolites showed that 4-C-3 is depleted in faecal and tumour samples from patients with CRC. 4-C-3 suppresses tumour growth in CRC cell lines, patient-derived organoids and xenografts. Mechanistically, 4-C-3 suppresses two major oncogenic drivers of CRC by inhibiting epidermal growth-factor receptor activation and stabilizing mutant oncogenic KRAS in an inactive state, thereby overcoming KRAS-driven resistance to anti-epidermal growth-factor receptor therapy. As proof of concept, restoring 4-C-3 using either Oscillibacter ruminantium, a natural 4-C-3 producer reduced in CRC, or a non-pathogenic Escherichia coli engineered to convert intestinal cholesterol into 4-C-3, lowered intratumoral cholesterol and induced tumour regression in preclinical models without overt toxicity. These findings uncover a microbiota–cholesterol metabolic pathway that can be harnessed through microbiome engineering to selectively target CRC and overcome therapy resistance. Modulation of intratumoral cholesterol metabolism through delivery of a microbiota-derived metabolite is shown to induce colorectal cancer regression in mice.

item.title: [1.9] RSK2 and β-Trcp-mediated ubiquitination of FOXN3 impairs DNA damage and confers radioresistance in lung cancer
item.description:
Aberrant DNA damage responses can result in genomic instability, thereby affecting the efficacy of radiotherapy. The transcription factor FOXN3 plays critical roles in cellular growth and proliferation, inflammation, and the response to injury; however, its involvement in lung cancer radioresistance remains unclear. Here, we revealed that reduced expression of FOXN3 was correlated with poor prognosis in lung adenocarcinoma patients and that FOXN3 depletion impaired the DNA damage response, thereby conferring radioresistance in lung cancer. Mechanistically, FOXN3 promoted BRCA1 transcription by binding to the BRCA1 promoter region, thereby increasing DNA damage. Furthermore, the protein kinase RSK2 and E3 ubiquitin ligase β-Trcp collaboratively interacted with FOXN3, facilitating its ubiquitination-mediated degradation via a conserved DSGYAS motif. Importantly, this cooperative degradation of FOXN3 attenuated DNA damage and promoted radioresistance in lung cancer cells. Our study provides a mechanistic foundation for targeting FOXN3-related pathways as a potential strategy to overcome radioresistance in lung cancer.

item.title: [1.9] Na+/Ca2+ exchanger 1 (NCX1) drives migration and vasculogenic mimicry in mesenchymal glioblastoma
item.description:
Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumor characterized by diffuse invasion, marked cellular plasticity, and poor prognosis, particularly in the mesenchymal subtype. The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger 1 (NCX1) has been implicated in glioblastoma motility, but its role in patient-derived mesenchymal GBM and vasculogenic mimicry (VM) remains unclear. Here, we investigated NCX1 function in GBM19, a primary mesenchymal glioblastoma stem cell-enriched culture. GBM19 cells displayed coordinated migration and formed Vascular Endothelial (VE)-cadherin-positive loop-like structures consistent with VM, whereas leading-edge cells showed a more migratory phenotype. NCX1 was enriched at the migratory front and was functionally active in both leading-edge and loop cells, as demonstrated by patch-clamp recordings and pharmacological inhibition with bepridil. NCX1 blockade impaired wound closure, disrupted actin organization, altered cell polarity and directional migration, reduced spheroid invasion, and prevented proper loop formation and closure. In vivo, VM-like tumor structures were positive for NCX1 and VE-cadherin. Transcriptomic analysis further showed a positive correlation between NCX1 and the VM-related regulator E74-like factor 2 (ELF2) specifically in mesenchymal GBM, where high ELF2 expression was associated with worse survival. These findings identify NCX1 as a regulator of migration and vasculogenic mimicry in mesenchymal glioblastoma and support its potential as a therapeutic target in aggressive GBM.

item.title: [1.7] B3GNT9-mediated O-glycosylation reprograms fatty acid metabolism in peroxisomes to promote invasion progression of peritumoral glioma cells
item.description:
Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumor characterized by rapid recurrence and invasion, particularly in the peritumoral brain zone (PBZ), a critical site for tumor spread. Through RNA-seq of tumor core and PBZ tissues from GBM patients, we identified B3GNT9 as significantly upregulated in tumor cells within the PBZ. Bioinformatics analysis revealed that elevated B3GNT9 expression is associated with poor prognosis. Functional studies in glioblastoma cell lines, patient-derived cells, and animal models showed that B3GNT9 overexpression promotes cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. Mechanistically, RNA-seq and in vitro experiments demonstrated that B3GNT9 enhances glioma invasiveness by regulating the fatty acid metabolism gene ACOX1. Quantitative proteomics further identified PPARD as a key transcription factor mediating the B3GNT9-ACOX1 signaling axis. B3GNT9 increases mucin-type O-glycosylation in glioblastoma cells, facilitating O-GalNAc glycosylation of PPARD, which enhances its transcriptional activity and drives ACOX1 expression. High-throughput metabolomics and cellular, organoid, and animal studies revealed that activation of the B3GNT9–PPARD–ACOX1 axis reduces intracellular eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) levels, promoting GBM invasiveness. These findings highlight the critical role of B3GNT9 and O-glycosylation in GBM progression, suggesting that targeting the B3GNT9–PPARD–ACOX1 axis could offer a promising therapeutic strategy to suppress GBM invasion and recurrence.

item.title: [1.7] EWSR1::ATF1 hyperactivation via TRIM11 depletion triggers lethal metabolic rewiring in clear cell sarcoma
item.description:
Clear cell sarcoma (CCS) is an ultra-rare and aggressive soft tissue sarcoma driven by the EWSR1::ATF1 fusion oncoprotein. Currently, no effective and well-tolerated treatment options are available to CCS patients. Direct inhibition of fusion transcription factors is precluded by the absence of defined ligand-binding pockets, whereas their abundance is under the control of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), offering an alternative avenue for biology-guided treatment. Here we show the abundance of EWSR1::ATF1 is tightly regulated by the UPS, and that release of this constraint is lethal to CCS cells. A reporter-based CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screen of UPS components identified TRIM11 as an E3 ligase that regulates turnover of EWSR1::ATF1, which it recognises as a neosubstrate without altering wild-type EWSR1 or ATF1. Depletion of TRIM11 increased nuclear fusion protein abundance, amplified the fusion-driven transcriptional programs and reduced viability. Proteomic analysis identified the cataplerotic enzyme phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 1 (PCK1), a direct EWSR1::ATF1 target, as the key mediator of lethal effects of fusion hyperactivation. Extracellular flux analysis, isotope tracing and quantitative metabolomics revealed excessive cataplerotic carbon withdrawal and impaired oxidative phosphorylation as the underlying mechanism. In patient tumors, high PCK1 expression associated with metastatic transcriptome programs and disease presentation, as well as shorter survival. Taken together, we report that hyperactivation of EWSR1::ATF1 opens a metabolic vulnerability, establishing TRIM11 as an actionable dependency and PCK1 as a candidate prognostic biomarker in CCS.

item.title: [2.0] Ultra-low-dose same-target combinations control drug resistance across stages
item.description:
The emergence of drug resistance continues to limit the long term effectiveness of cancer therapies [1], as tumour cells adapt to therapeutic selective pressure through diverse genetic and non-genetic routes [2,3]. Despite advances in more potent and next generation inhibitors and mechanism based combination therapies [4,5], durable disease control remains difficult to achieve. Here we tested an alternative strategy: combining multiple inhibitors directed against the same oncogenic driver, each at ultra low doses with minimal individual activity, to delay resistance emergence. In epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) driven cancer models, such ultra low dose same target combinations (ULDCs) distributed individually weak perturbations across multiple inhibitors directed against the same target and achieved substantial growth inhibition in vitro and antitumour activity in vivo despite weak effects of the corresponding single agents. Under similar levels of growth inhibition (~50%), single-agent EGFR inhibitors generated resistant outgrowth, whereas a five drug ULDC delayed resistance emergence. Increasing the number of inhibitors further delayed resistance emergence, with no detectable resistant outgrowth observed for combinations containing 8 to 14 inhibitors within the experimental timeframe. The five drug ULDC also retained measurable growth inhibitory activity against gefitinib resistant PC-9/GR cells, and resistant cells arising under five drug ULDC treatment exhibited markedly greater reversibility following drug withdrawal than those arising under single agent treatment. Although pharmacological additivity or synergy may contribute to the collective growth inhibitory effects of ULDCs, the divergent long term resistance outcomes observed under similar levels of growth inhibition indicate that resistance behaviour is not determined by inhibitory strength alone. Instead, our findings support a model in which increasing same target inhibitor diversity progressively constrains the adaptive trajectories available during resistance evolution, while therapeutic perturbation architecture may also influence the stability of resistant states that emerge. More broadly, these findings support the concept of same target collective suppression, in which multiple individually weak perturbations directed against the same target can collectively produce substantial antitumour activity and constrain resistance evolution across multiple stages. We propose that increasing same target inhibitor diversity may restrict accessible adaptive trajectories, while therapeutic perturbation architecture may also influence the stability of resistant states.

item.title: [2.4] Developing a Multimodal miR-15a Mimic to Overcome Gemcitabine and RAS(ON) Inhibitor Daraxonrasib Resistance in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
item.description:
Gemcitabine remains a mainstay of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) treatment, while the RAS(ON) inhibitor daraxonrasib has recently demonstrated improved survival in previously treated metastatic disease. However, acquired resistance to both therapies remains a major clinical challenge. Here, we developed MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a, a multimodal microRNA (miRNA)-based therapeutic, by chemically modifying tumor-suppressive miR-15a with methotrexate (MTX), 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), and gemcitabine (Gem) to combine sequence-specific gene regulation with disruption of nucleotide metabolism. MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a exhibited low-nanomolar potency across five PDAC cell lines and retained activity in gemcitabine- and daraxonrasib-resistant models under vehicle-free conditions, substantially exceeding that of stoichiometrically matched free antimetabolites. Treatment induced S-phase accumulation, increased DNA damage and apoptosis, and suppressed checkpoint and survival-associated proteins, including WEE1, CHK1, YAP1, and BCL-2. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses revealed increased DNA replication, replication-stress, and repair-associated programs, together with reduced oncogenic signaling. In gemcitabine-resistant cells, treatment restored the gemcitabine-activating enzyme dCK, reduced ABCC1 and ABCC3 expression, and suppressed resistance-associated signaling programs, indicating partial remodeling of resistance-associated pathways. MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a also synergized with daraxonrasib (mean Bliss synergy score, 22.52) and activated tumor-cell-intrinsic STING-TBK1 signaling, accompanied by increased interferon stimulated gene expression and IFN-{beta} and CXCL10 secretion. Finally, MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a retained low-nanomolar potency in three patient-derived PDAC organoids and significantly suppressed metastatic tumor growth in vivo at 4 mg/kg. Together, these findings support a multimodal miRNA therapeutic strategy that combines replication-associated DNA damage, checkpoint protein suppression, and innate immune activation-associated responses to target therapeutic resistance in PDAC.

item.title: [2.0] Miniaturized Traceless Staudinger Ligation Enables Direct-to-Biology Screening of Potent BRD4 PROTACs
item.description:
Direct-to-biology (D2B) approaches accelerate PROTAC discovery by enabling biological screening of crude reaction mixtures without intermediate purification. However, the range of chemical transformations compatible with these workflows remains limited. Herein, we establish a miniaturized, base-free traceless Staudinger ligation platform diversifying linker chemistry for a preexisting library of E3-ligand-linker adducts bearing azide moieties. As a proof-of-concept target, BRD4 was chosen, yielding amide-linked BRD4-targeting PROTACs. By combining phosphine-functionalized JQ1 derivatives with 72 selected azide building blocks, reactions were performed on a 5 L scale in 384-well plates, achieving a mean LC-MS conversion of approximately 65%. Spiking experiments confirmed that the phosphine starting materials had no significant impact on BRD4 degradation, supporting the direct biological evaluation of crude reaction mixtures in the presence of residual starting material. Cellular screening identified 23 hits at 250 nM screening concentration, reducing BRD4 levels below 40%. Two resynthesized and purified PROTACs were subsequently validated, displaying pDC50 values of 8.2 and 7.0 and a Dmax of 90% and 96%, respectively. This work establishes traceless Staudinger ligation as a complementary D2B strategy for the rapid discovery of amide-linked PROTACs.

item.title: [2.2] ZNF598 promotes glioblastoma progression and temozolomide resistance by facilitating MFN1-mediated mitochondrial quality control
item.description:
Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive primary brain tumor and frequently develops intrinsic or acquired resistance to temozolomide (TMZ). Mitochondrial quality control (MQC) is essential for tumor cell survival and therapeutic adaptation, yet its upstream regulatory mechanisms in GBM remain poorly defined. Here, we identify zinc finger protein 598 (ZNF598), an E3 ubiquitin ligase with RNA-binding capacity, as a critical regulator of MQC and TMZ resistance in GBM. Analysis of public datasets revealed that ZNF598 expression is significantly elevated in TMZ-resistant GBM cells and human glioma tissues, correlating with adverse patient prognosis. Functionally, ZNF598 knockdown suppressed GBM cell proliferation, induced apoptosis, and disrupted mitochondrial homeostasis, as reflected by reduced ATP production and mtDNA copy numbers, elevated reactive oxygen species, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, and mitochondrial fragmentation. ZNF598 silencing suppressed tumor growth in subcutaneous and intracranial orthotopic xenograft models and markedly enhanced TMZ sensitivity in vitro and in subcutaneous xenografts. Mechanistically, ZNF598 associated with mitofusin 1 (MFN1) mRNA and maintained its stability, thereby sustaining MFN1 expression and MFN1-mediated mitochondrial fusion. item.title: [1.5] Conditional biologics in cancer immunotherapy: mechanisms, applications and clinical progress
item.description:
Immunotherapy has transformed cancer treatment, enabling durable responses and long-term survival in many patients. However, widespread use remains limited by refractory indications, immune-related toxicities and acquired resistance. Complications such as cytokine release syndrome, immune-related adverse events, infusion-related reactions and on-target, off-tumour toxicities have emerged as specific safety concerns. We describe the landscape of KDM inhibitors, especially LSD1 inhibitors, which are the most advanced demethylase inhibitors in clinical trials. We highlight the need for more potent and selective KDM inhibitors, biomarkers of therapeutic response, novel combinatorial treatments and innovative drug discovery strategies. item.title: [2.5] Targeting mutant p53 aggregates in pancreatic cancer using an autophagy-targeting chimera

Protein aggregation is increasingly recognized as a fundamental feature of cancer biology, particularly in tumors experiencing chronic proteotoxic stress. TP53 is one of the most frequently mutated genes in human cancers, and many cancer-associated missense mutations promote p53 misfolding and amyloid-like aggregation. These aggregates impair wild-type tumor-suppressive functions while conferring oncogenic gain-of-function (GOF) activities that promote tumor progression and therapeutic resistance. item.title: [2.5] Positional replication fork instability drives PARP inhibitor cytotoxicity
item.description:
Although poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) show promise for treating homologous recombination-deficient cancers, the observed PARPi hypersensitivity in additional genetic contexts expands their potential use in precision oncology. Yet, the DNA lesions driving PARPi-induced cytotoxicity remain poorly defined. Here we uncover distinct replication-fork lesions in specific genomic regions as key determinants of PARPi cytotoxicity. Using CRISPR screens, we identify that loss of replication-coupled cohesin acetyltransferase ESCO2 confers PARPi hypersensitivity independently of homologous recombination deficiency. Quantitative single-molecule imaging reveals that ESCO2 loss promotes accumulation of G-quadruplex (G4) DNA structures at a subset of replication-associated sites, associated with PARP1 activation and engagement of fork protection factor TIMELESS to mitigate G4-induced stress. Notably, these G4 lesions localize to fragile pericentromeric regions and engage the G4 helicase DDX11. PARP inhibition disrupts this protective G4-processing response by preventing PARP1-dependent engagement of TIMELESS and DDX11, leading to G4 accumulation, DNA damage and chromosomal instability. Together, our findings define the G4–PARP1–TIMELESS–DDX11 axis as a critical safeguard of replication fork stability at hard-to-replicate loci and reveal ESCO2 as a therapeutic target for promoting synthetic lethality in PARPi-treated cancers. item.title: [2.3] ENPP1 inhibits the cGAS–STING pathway to mediate immune evasion in EGFR-TKI–resistant non–small cell lung cancer
item.description:
Third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), such as osimertinib, have demonstrated promising clinical efficacy in the treatment of EGFR-mutant non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Despite substantial progress with EGFR-TKIs, the development of acquired resistance remains a major clinical challenge. Notably, the addition of immune checkpoint blockade after TKI resistance has not resulted in significant survival benefits compared to chemotherapy. In this study, we performed a comprehensive transcriptomic analysis of established osimertinib-resistant tumor models and found that the expression of the ectonucleotide phosphodiesterase ENPP1, a key regulator of extracellular cGAMP signaling, was significantly upregulated in resistant tumors compared to the parental TKI-sensitive NSCLC tumors. Mechanistically, upregulated ENPP1 in resistant cells promoted the hydrolysis of extracellular cGAMP, suppressing the cGAS–STING pathway in immune cells and subsequently impairing immune cell activation and function, thereby promoting immune suppression and tumor progression. Genetic depletion or pharmacological inhibition of ENPP1 enhanced immune cell–mediated cytotoxicity against TKI-resistant tumor cells. Furthermore, the use of ENPP1 inhibitors both in vitro and in vivo enhanced immune cell activity and antitumor efficacy in TKI-resistant lung cancers with high ENPP1 expression. Importantly, these observations were further validated by paired clinical tumor samples, which demonstrated increased ENPP1 expression following the development of acquired EGFR-TKI resistance. Collectively, our study highlights a critical role for ENPP1 in mediating immune evasion through suppression of the cGAMP–STING pathway in the tumor immune microenvironment, supporting ENPP1 as a promising therapeutic target to enhance immunotherapy efficacy in EGFR-TKI–resistant NSCLC.

item.title: [1.9] Novel formula for improving the oral bioavailability of paclitaxel using P-glycoprotein inhibitors
item.description:
Paclitaxel (PCL), a taxane derivative with potent antimitotic properties, is ubiquitously utilized as a remedy for various cancers. PCL’s therapeutic utility via the oral route is limited by poor water solubility and low permeability, resulting in inadequate bioavailability. This limitation restricts the development of effective oral formulations, particularly for conditions such as gastric cancer. The current research aimed to evaluate the effects of P-glycoprotein (P-gp) inhibitors, specifically piperine (PIP) and silibinin (SBN), on the pharmacokinetic parameters of orally administered PCL. An in-silico drug-protein docking study was performed to evaluate interactions between PCL and selected P-gp inhibitors. PCL was administered orally at a dose of 40 mg/kg, either as a single treatment or in combination with PIP or SBN at 10, 20, and 40 mg/kg. item.title: [1.6] USP14-mediated deubiquitination stabilizes integrin β1 to sustain malignant progression and chemotherapy resistance in osteosarcoma
item.description:
Osteosarcoma patients with metastasis or chemotherapy resistance typically have a poor prognosis, yet the precise mechanisms underlying these adverse clinical outcomes remain elusive. In this study, we analyzed tissue proteomic data from our osteosarcoma cohort to compare protein expression profiles between metastatic and non-metastatic cases, as well as subgroups with low versus high chemotherapy-induced tumor necrosis rates. Our clinical analyses revealed that elevated ubiquitin-specific protease 14 (USP14) expression was associated with lung metastasis, a lower tumor necrosis rate, and shorter overall survival. Functional experiments in vitro and in vivo demonstrated that USP14 knockdown robustly suppressed the proliferation and metastatic potential of osteosarcoma cells. Mechanistically, USP14 interacted with and stabilized integrin β1 via deubiquitination, thereby activating the FAK/SRC axis and inducing inhibitory  phosphorylation of GSK3β. This signaling cascade blocked β-catenin ubiquitin-dependent degradation to promote β-catenin accumulation, nuclear translocation, and subsequent activation of TCF/LEF-mediated transcription of downstream oncogenes, ultimately driving osteosarcoma progression. Moreover, chemotherapy upregulated USP14 expression, thereby promoting chemoresistance. Pharmacological inhibition of USP14 with IU1 synergistically enhanced the chemosensitivity of osteosarcoma cells to doxorubicin, effectively restraining tumor growth and metastasis. Collectively, our findings delineate a core USP14-driven oncogenic cascade governing osteosarcoma progression, highlighting USP14 as a promising therapeutic target to improve chemotherapy efficacy and clinical outcomes for osteosarcoma patients.

item.title: [1.7] Dingxiang Guanshitong suppresses ESCC progression by modulating TAK1/NF-κB/GLUT1-associated glycolytic reprogramming
item.description:
Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is a highly aggressive tumor with poor clinical outcomes and limited treatment options. Dingxiang Guanshitong (DGST), a traditional Chinese herbal formulation, has shown potential activity in ESCC, but its molecular mechanisms require further clarification. The current study aimed to evaluate the therapeutic impact and underlying biological actions of DGST on ESCC. Network pharmacology was used to identify candidate DGST constituents and targets, followed by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis. Antitumor effects of DGST was examined in a 4-nitroquinoline 1-oxide (4NQO)-induced ESCC mouse model using H&E staining, immunohistochemistry, TUNEL assay, and flow cytometry. Proteomics analysis identified differentially expressed proteins and enriched pathways. In TE-1 cells, TAK1 knockdown/overexpression stable lines were constructed by lentiviral transduction, and pathway involvement was evaluated using immunofluorescence, luciferase reporter assays, CCK-8, Transwell, scratch assays, qRT-PCR, western blotting, and metabolic indicator assays. DGST showed dose-associated suppression of ESCC tumor progression, cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, while promoting apoptosis. Proteomics suggested that DGST affected glycolysis and NF-κB-related pathways. DGST treatment was associated with reduced phosphorylation of TAK1, IκBα, and p65, lower GLUT1, HK2, PFKP, and LDHA expression, decreased ATP levels, and increased MPC1 as well as mitochondrial complex indicators. TAK1 knockdown enhanced the effects of DGST, whereas its overexpression reversed these effects. DGST may inhibit ESCC progression by modulating TAK1/NF-κB/GLUT1 axis-mediated glycolytic reprogramming. The findings elucidate the potential therapeutic value of DGST in the treatment of ESCC and provide mechanistic insights for its clinical application.

item.title: [1.8] MET inhibition exploits conserved regulatory dependencies in malignant rhabdoid tumors
item.description:
Malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs) are lethal, yet genomically simple childhood cancers characterised by universal SWI/SNF dysregulation. Despite this shared molecular framework, the regulatory programs sustaining MRTs and how they wire actionable dependencies, remain poorly defined. Here, we integrated single-cell multi-omic profiling and spatial transcriptomics across anatomically and molecularly diverse MRTs, generating a comprehensive multimodal MRT dataset at single-cell resolution. We leveraged this resource to identify candidate tumor-specific dependencies, which were subsequently functionally validated in vitro and in vivo in matched patient-derived models. We found that distinct malignant subpopulations are spatially patterned in complex environmentally shaped topologies, consistent with reciprocal interactions with stromal and immune compartments contributing to intratumoral transcriptional diversity. We identified recurrent transcriptional metaprograms conserved across patients and molecular subtypes, including a previously undescribed shared core rhabdoid program, as well as a metaprogram characterized by extracellular matrix interactions, and preferentially localized in tumor-stroma intermixed neighborhoods, supporting identification of niche conditioning cues. Mechanistically, we identified regulatory wiring driving these metaprograms, with the core shared rhabdoid programme coordinated by a circuit centred on TCF12, ZNF148 and CHD2. Guided by target nominations from our integrated analyses, we performed a curated drug screen using patient-derived MRT models and validated HGF/MET signaling as a selective vulnerability in extrarenal rhabdoid tumors. Pharmacologic MET inhibition was cytotoxic in sensitive models and induced a complete response in vivo using a clinically approved compound. Importantly, MET expression in primary tumors correlated with response, supporting biomarker-guided patient stratification for immediate clinical translation. Collectively, our findings define the molecular architecture of MRTs, reveal conserved regulatory programs beyond anatomical and molecular subtypes, and highlight a targetable signaling axis with immediate translational potential, establishing a framework for precision therapy in this lethal pediatric malignancy.

item.title: [1.9] Glioblastoma model mouse rescue from mortality by brain-targeted catalytically-enhanced angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 mutant-antibody fusion protein
item.description:
We have discovered that an engineered angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2)-brain-targeted antibody fusion protein, referred to as ACE2dm-s1, improves survival of CT-2A xenograft glioblastoma (GBM) model mice when administered in combination with a small molecule STING agonist cancer therapeutic. item.title: [1.9] Alpha-aminoadipate in the saccharopine pathway promotes cancer metastasis through sumoylation of transcription machinery
item.description:
Despite studies linking metabolism and cancer, our understanding of the metabolite network that drives metastasis remains incomplete. Through a metabolic RNAi-based screen for cell invasion, we identify alpha-aminoadipate (2-AAA), the intermediate metabolite of aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase (AASS) in the saccharopine pathway, as a common pivotal factor in metastasis of human cancers. Metabolite-protein connectivity mapping reveals that 2-AAA binds to SAE1, a crucial component of the SUMO-activating enzyme E1, and enhances SAE1 recruitment to UBA2, facilitating sumoylation. 2-AAA-mediated sumoylation of the RNA polymerase subunit POLR2A then partially promotes cancer cell invasion by inducing the expression of metastasis-promoting genes, including SPG11 and KCTD7. Our study highlights the mechanism by which metastasis is mediated by metabolite-driven sumoylation and indicates AASS as an effective therapeutic target for mitigating metastatic cancer progression. The role of metabolism in metastasis remains unclear. item.title: [1.6] Death pathway plasticity in therapy resistance: mechanistic switches and translational opportunities
item.description:
Regulated cell death (RCD) programs in cancer have traditionally been framed as discrete pathways defined by signature effectors, including caspases (apoptosis), RIPK1–RIPK3–MLKL (necroptosis), gasdermins (pyroptosis), lipid peroxidation control nodes (ferroptosis), PARP1–AIF/MIF (parthanatos), and FDX1-dependent lipoylation stress (cuproptosis). Here, we advance an integrated view in which these programs function as a configurable decision network rather than isolated routes. Therapeutic and microenvironmental inputs, such as death ligands, chemoradiotherapy, targeted agents, PARP inhibition, copper ionophores, nutrient/oxidative stress, extracellular matrix detachment, and cytotoxic T-cell pressure, converge on shared hub modules that act as rheostats, routing cells toward distinct execution outcomes or into drug-tolerant persister states. This circuit-level framing explains context-dependent switching and mixed phenotypes, including caspase-8/c-FLIP control of apoptosis–necroptosis, caspase–gasdermin coupling of apoptosis–pyroptosis, and metabolic–redox tuning of ferroptosis susceptibility via SLC7A11–GPX4–ACSL4–FSP1 and autophagy-linked lipid/iron handling. We outline a biomarker and functional assay framework to map tumor death wiring from biopsies and organoid challenges, enabling rational combination strategies that exploit death program plasticity while anticipating resistance and inflammatory toxicities.

item.title: [1.9] PD-L1 is associated with metabolic adaptation and mitochondrial remodeling in NSCLC cells
item.description:
Tumor metabolism is governed by a complex network of processes that can influence immune evasion. Metabolic dysregulation in tumor cells can lead to the accumulation of metabolites that may influence immune cell function. However, the relationship between PD-L1 expression and tumor cell metabolism remains incompletely understood. Here, we report that PD-L1 expression in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells is associated with increased endocytic activity and altered metabolic flux, particularly in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. PD-L1 expression is aleo associated with mitochondrial remodeling, including alterations in proteins involved in mitochondrial fusion and fission and in mitochondrial respiratory chain components. Integrated multi-omics analyses further identified differential H3K9me3 patterns associated with differences in PD-L1 expression status, including differential H3K9me3 patterns at the PTPRN2 locus. Collectively, our findings suggest that differences in PD-L1 expression status are associated with metabolic, mitochondrial, and epigenetic alterations in NSCLC cells.

item.title: [2.0] Perioperative ivonescimab with or without chemotherapy in resectable non-small cell lung cancer: a phase 2 trial
item.description:
Resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) carries a high risk of postoperative recurrence, underscoring the need for effective perioperative therapies. This nonrandomized, noncomparative phase 2 trial evaluated neoadjuvant ivonescimab monotherapy (cohort 1) or in combination with chemotherapy (cohort 2), followed by surgery and adjuvant ivonescimab. In cohort 2, the major pathological response (MPR) rate was 70.1% (47/67; 95% confidence interval (CI) = 57.7–80.7); the lower bound of the 80% two-sided CI exceeded the historical control rate of 41% and the primary endpoint was met. The MPR rate in cohort 1 was 60.0% (6/10; 95% CI = 26.2–87.8). Among patients who achieved MPR, 83.3% (5/6) in cohort 1 and 97.9% (46/47) in cohort 2 had residual viable tumor (RVT) of ≤5%, respectively. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events (AEs) occurred in 36.4% (4/11) patients in cohort 1 and 30.4% (24/79) of those in cohort 2, with no grade 3 or higher hemorrhage or treatment-related death. Treatment-related surgery delay occurred in one (1.3%) patient. Surgery-related AEs related to ivonescimab occurred in 10.0% (1/10) and 10.4% (7/67) patients in the two cohorts, respectively, with no grade 3 or higher events reported. These data support perioperative ivonescimab with or without chemotherapy as a promising strategy for resectable NSCLC. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05247684 . In a nonrandomized phase 2 trial, patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer received perioperative ivonescimab as monotherapy or with chemotherapy, leading to encouraging pathological response rates in both cohorts, and sustained circulating tumor DNA negativity throughout neoadjuvant therapy may be predictive of response.

item.title: [1.9] Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
item.description:
Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment1–8, suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear9–13. Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance. Multi-omic analyses of cells from patients with glioblastoma (GB) provide insight into the role of non-genetic cellular plasticity in disease progression, showing that state stability in GB cells is controlled by a network of interacting activators and repressors.

item.title: [1.5] Early Progression Cells mark a stem-like state associated with pancreatic cancer initiation and progression
item.description:
Pancreatic cancer is deemed to progress from microscopic pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanINs). However, low grade PanINs are frequently detected in the general population without presentation or increased risk of developing cancer, suggesting that many PanINs never progress to tumours. What precisely characterises PanINs that develop into tumours is insufficiently understood. Using a mouse model where pancreatitis-induced tissue injury promotes pancreatic cancer from rare KrasG12D cells, we identify Early Progression Cells (EPCs) as a new entity, a novel population of cancer stem-like cells. Transcriptomic analyses illustrate EPCs as stress-adapted, inflammation responsive stem cells that also upregulate gene programmes indicative of microenvironment remodelling. Using identified EPC protein markers, we show that EPCs are prevalent in early metaplastic stages and in PanIN progression from low grade to high grade but are rarer in tumours. PanIN- and tumour-derived sphere and organoid assays demonstrate that EPCs possess all characteristics of stem cells in vitro and are dependent on Nupr1 stress response pathways for survival and growth. We identify APP-CD74 as a novel cell-cell interaction pathway between EPCs and neighbouring epithelial cells in PanINs and tumours. Inhibition of CD74 activity in vitro induces high-grade PanIN organoid death, suggesting EPCs are critical for high-grade PanINs. Using spatial transcriptomics of human samples, we detect gene signatures of EPCs in distinct regions of human PanIN and PDAC tissues, including APP-CD74 interactions, providing compelling evidence that EPCs are relevant to human disease. Further understanding of EPC biology will likely uncover new knowledge on why rare PanINs progress towards tumours.

item.title: [1.5] Coupled Modeling of Tumor Volume and ctDNA Dynamics in HPV-Associated Anal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
item.description:
Response to anti-PD-1 immunotherapy in advanced HPV-associated anal squamous cell carcinoma (ASCC) varies and is assessed by infrequent imaging that lags behind tumor biology. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) can be sampled frequently and reflects near-real-time tumor activity yet is rarely built into mechanistic models of treatment response. Using longitudinal tumor volume and HPV ctDNA from 26 patients treated with pembrolizumab, we found that baseline ctDNA scores tracked tumor burden but did not distinguish responders from non-responders, whereas ctDNA after one treatment cycle had a higher relative decrease in responders, six weeks before the next scan. Sensitivity, identifiability, and model-selection analyses reduced it to two patient-specific parameters, proliferation and shedding rates, which reproduced individual volume and ctDNA trajectories, including a transient ctDNA spike at treatment onset. item.title: [2.1] AMD1-driven MTA production sustains chemoresistance by rewiring PMN-MDSC immunosuppression
item.description:
Chemoresistance reflects both tumor cell-intrinsic adaptation and remodeling of the immune microenvironment. However, the mechanisms by which chemoresistant tumor cells orchestrate and sustain an immunosuppressive microenvironment remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that chemoresistant tumors exhibit marked accumulation of polymorphonuclear myeloid-derived suppressor cells (PMN-MDSCs), which exert potent immunosuppressive effects on CD8+T cells and are critical for drug resistance. Metabolomic profiling reveals that resistant tumor cells release the metabolite 5'-methylthioadenosine (MTA). MTA enhances the immunosuppressive function of PMN-MDSCs by bolstering JAK-STAT3 signaling. Mechanistically, MTA binds to the protein tyrosine phosphatase PTPN2 to block its phosphatase activity, thereby potentiating activation of JAK-STAT3 signaling pathway. Moreover, we uncover that adenosylmethionine decarboxylase 1 (AMD1) is the key metabolic determinant of MTA accumulation in chemoresistant tumor cells. Genetic or pharmacological AMD1 inhibition significantly decreases MTA level, diminishes PMN-MDSC immunosuppressive function, and re-sensitizes the resistant tumors to chemotherapy and immunotherapy. item.title: [1.9] Preliminary results and clinical experiences of [177Lu]Lu-FAP-2286 for brain metastases in advanced lung cancer
item.description:
Brain metastases in advanced lung cancer present a therapeutic challenge with limited effective options. Fibroblast activation protein (FAP) is overexpressed in cancer-associated fibroblasts within brain metastatic lesions, making it a promising target for radionuclide therapy. This prospective study evaluated the intracranial efficacy and safety of peptide-targeted radionuclide therapy (PTRT) with [177Lu]Lu-FAP-2286 in 14 patients with FAP-expressing advanced lung cancer and radiologically confirmed brain metastases who had failed prior treatments. Patients received [177Lu]Lu-FAP-2286 (7.4 GBq/cycle, ≥ 2 cycles). Intracranial objective response rate was 57.1% and disease control rate was 92.9% by RECIST 1.1, with a metabolic response rate of 64.3% by PERCIST 1.0. Median overall survival was 11.0 months and median progression-free survival was 8.0 months. Patients achieving metabolic response had significantly longer survival. Neurological symptoms and brain-specific quality of life improved significantly, and no grade III/IV adverse events occurred. These findings suggest that systemic [177Lu]Lu-FAP-2286 PTRT is safe and effective for brain metastases in FAP-expressing advanced lung cancer, achieving intracranial tumor regression, symptom relief, and improved quality of life, thereby offering a promising therapeutic option for this refractory population.

item.title: [2.1] HER3 mediates metabolic reprogramming in metastatic colorectal and pancreatic cancer
item.description:
Liver metastases are a major cause of mortality in colorectal cancer (CRC) and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), yet the oncogenic signals that shape tumor metabolism in the hepatic niche remain poorly understood. Here, we show that HER3 activation drives a liver metastasis-specific glycolytic program in both cancer types. Genetic or pharmacological HER3 inhibition suppresses cancer glycolysis while increasing dependence on oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), rendering liver metastases vulnerable to OXPHOS inhibition. Combining the HER3 inhibitor sapitinib with distinct OXPHOS inhibitors led to in vitro synergy and durable tumor-free survival in orthotopic CRC and PDAC liver metastases models, with further validation in patient-derived xenografts. Mechanistically, HER3 promotes glycolysis through activating PFK2 and reduces OXPHOS through activating DRP1-mediated mitochondrial remodeling, both pathways were activated in liver metastases compared to matched primary tumors. Together, our findings identify the HER3-AKT/RSK-PFK2 axis as a driver of glycolysis and metastatic growth and reveal an OXPHOS dependency induced by HER3 inhibition that may be exploited through combined HER3 and OXPHOS targeting in metastatic CRC and PDAC.

item.title: [1.6] SDHB deficiency silences ABCB1 expression and confers therapeutic vulnerability across multiple cancer types
item.description:
Succinate dehydrogenase B (SDHB)-deficient cancers, including pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL), renal cell carcinoma (RCC), and gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST), exhibit aggressive clinical behavior with limited treatment options. To identify novel therapeutic vulnerabilities, we performed high-throughput drug screening using co-cultured human SDHB-deficient and SDHB-reconstituted UOK269 human renal cell carcinoma cells with dual fluorescence labeling. Several compounds displaying preferential cytotoxicity toward SDHB-deficient cells were known substrates of the ATP-binding cassette B1 (ABCB1) transporter, also known as Multidrug Resistance Protein 1 (MDR1). Accordingly, SDHB-deficient cells demonstrated markedly reduced ABCB1 expression, a phenotype confirmed across human SDHB-deficient PPGL, RCC, and GIST samples, but absent in IDH- or FH-deficient tumors. Mechanistic investigation revealed that KDM4A histone demethylase is downregulated in SDHB-deficient tumors, and KDM4A loss (or inhibition) is sufficient to reduce ABCB1 expression, globally increase H3K9me3 levels, and sensitize cells to cytotoxic ABCB1 substrates. TCGA analysis confirmed correlated KDM4A-ABCB1 expression in SDHB-deficient cancers, with ABCB1 levels predicting drug sensitivity across cancer cell lines. Clinical analysis demonstrated that SDHB-mutant PPGL patients treated with vincristine-containing chemotherapy exhibited significantly longer progression-free survival compared to non-SDHB patients. These findings establish a novel metabolic-epigenetic pathway linking SDHB deficiency to ABCB1 silencing and provide rational basis for repurposing vincristine, and related ABCB1 substrate vinca alkaloids, across SDHB-deficient cancer types; offering an alternative precision treatment approach for these challenging malignancies.
